summary: A paper presenting a classification of email routing issues. It organizes the different problems of getting mail from sender to recipient across varied networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A way of sorting the different puzzles that come up when mail has to find its way to the right mailbox.

questions: how is mail routed across networks
difference between static and dynamic mail routing
subtitle: A taxonomy of email routing strategies for distributed mail systems

tldr.problem: Email operators and system managers lack a common vocabulary for discussing routing strategies, making it difficult to compare systems, choose approaches, and debug routing problems across different mail platforms.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines and classifies email routing along multiple dimensions: static versus dynamic routing, direct versus indirect routing, firewall and default-route patterns, routing control, bulk routing, source routing, and routing communities.
tldr.outcome: Mail system managers gained a standard reference for understanding routing options, comparing different email platforms, and making informed decisions about their messaging infrastructure.

today: RFC 1711 is Informational and remains a foundational reference for understanding email routing. While email technology has evolved—SPF, DKIM, and DMARC now influence routing decisions—the core routing patterns and terminology defined in RFC 1711 are still in use today.

sections.title: Naming, Addressing, and Routing
sections.content:
Email routing involves three distinct concepts: names uniquely identify a person or recipient, addresses tell where that person is located, and routes describe the path a message takes to reach them. An email address typically has two parts: a domain-related part (like the domain name in RFC 822 email or an ADMD in X.400), and a local or user-related part (like the part before the @ sign in email).

The document defines an e-mail route as a path between two Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) for one sender-recipient pair. User Agents (UAs) represent the actual people sending and reading mail. If a message is redirected at the UA level, a new route is established. Routes are not bidirectional; a reply may travel a completely different path due to cost, network topology, load, or policy.

Routing is inherently a distributed process. Every MTA along the path makes its own routing decision, looking up the address in a routing database to find possible next hops. The database might be table-based, rule-based, or directory-based. The decision is not purely algorithmic; the same address might lead to different routes depending on system availability, network congestion, and other factors.
sections.eli5: Email travels through multiple mail systems, and each one decides where to send it next by looking up the address in its own routing tables or rules.

sections.title: Static and Dynamic Routing
sections.content:
Static routing uses fixed routing tables that do not adapt to external conditions like system availability or network load. It is the simplest form of routing but inflexible. Dynamic routing allows routing decisions to adapt based on real-time conditions: choosing among multiple Mail eXchanger (MX) records in the Internet's DNS, using fallback MTAs if the primary is unavailable, or selecting different network stacks for underlying transport.

Dynamic routing operates at multiple layers. At the mail level, an MTA can choose among multiple MTAs that serve a domain, each with priority rankings. At the stack level, an MTA might prefer to contact a peer over TCP/IP but fall back to X.25 if necessary. Table-based routing need not be purely static; for example, X.400 routing under RFC 1465 is table-based but allows dynamic selection of backup relay MTAs.

For flexibility and reliability, dynamic routing is almost always preferred in practice. However, dynamic routing introduces complexity and potential for loops. All MTAs in a community cannot use pure default routing; at least one must know the full set of routing rules to detect when an address cannot be delivered and generate an error message rather than passing it in circles.
sections.eli5: Static routing sends every message the same way no matter what. Dynamic routing picks the best path based on what systems are available right now.

sections.title: Direct and Indirect Routing
sections.content:
Direct routing allows one MTA to contact another MTA directly; this requires a fully meshed network where every MTA knows about every other MTA. Indirect routing (store-and-forward) uses intermediate MTAs as relays. Most real-world email uses some degree of indirect routing because fully meshed networks do not scale.

Firewalls implement downstream indirection. A firewall MTA "attracts" all messages for a set of addresses from the outside email world and relays them into a protected network. The outside MTAs publish routes to the firewall, which then uses local knowledge to deliver mail within the protected domain. Internet mail uses Mail eXchangers (MX records) as firewalls; many domains hide behind one or more MX records to concentrate mail management.

Default routes implement upstream indirection. An MTA sends all unroutable messages to a single trusted MTA (the default route) to handle delivery. This is typically used with a firewall in the opposite direction: messages leaving a domain go to the firewall, which then routes them to the wider network. The simplest default algorithm is to first check for local users, then default-route everything else.
sections.eli5: Some email systems send mail directly between servers (if you know where everyone is), while others use relay servers in the middle to make things simpler.

sections.title: User-Level Routing and Communities
sections.content:
Normally, routing proceeds down to the domain level, and all mail for users in that domain is delivered locally by default. But distributed domains occur when users in the same domain have mailboxes on different MTAs. One solution is to create subdomains for each platform and route accordingly. Another is to route based on the local part of the address (the user name) in addition to the domain. Some email systems handle user-level routing better than others.

Shared MTAs host multiple domains on the same system. This creates potential conflicts when different domains have users with the same name, though this is solved in practice by maintaining per-domain user databases.

A routing community is a set of MTAs that agree on common routing rules. The Internet mail community is the largest, using DNS-based routing rules. The Internet mail community is open: any MTA meeting basic requirements can participate, and routing information is public. Other communities are closed (like internal corporate X.400 systems), hierarchical (organized in a tree), or local (single MTA perspective). Gateway MTAs often belong to multiple communities simultaneously.
sections.eli5: Email domains can be split across multiple mail servers, and groups of mail servers that agree on routing rules together form communities like the Internet or corporate X.400 systems.

sections.title: Routing Control, Bulk Routing, and Source Routing
sections.content:
Routing control allows the message originator or intermediate MTAs to affect routing decisions, granting or denying access for certain users or groups. In X.400 systems, routing control can restrict messages to certain providers or prevent routing of international traffic. However, routing control makes the messaging environment unpredictable for users; when used, senders should receive clear explanations of why their message was rejected and how to avoid future rejections.

Bulk routing reduces network traffic by transferring a message addressed to multiple users to a remote domain only once, then "exploding" it into separate copies at the destination. This is especially valuable when an MTA hosts large mailing lists. In hierarchical firewall systems, this happens almost automatically. In direct routing environments like BITNET, the MTA needs topology knowledge to route efficiently; BITNET uses a special distribute protocol to select topology-aware servers.

Source routing lets users specify a route through MTAs. Explicit source routing (like @mta1:@mta2:user@domain) encodes the path in the address; each MTA strips itself and forwards. Address routing uses gateway-assigned paths automatically. In modern Internet mail, explicit source routing is discouraged because the Internet is now fully interconnected; the need to know network topology has vanished. However, automatic source routing (like address translation at gateways) remains useful for interoperability between mail systems.
sections.eli5: Administrators can control who sends mail where, bundle multiple messages together to save bandwidth, or specify the exact path a message should take through multiple relays.

sections.title: Routing in Deployed Systems
sections.content:
The document surveys routing strategies in real email systems. Internet mail (RFC 822) uses DNS-based dynamic routing, mostly direct topology, supports distributed domains and shared MTAs, and is an open routing community. UUCP uses static routing with "bang" addressing (poor man's routing), mostly indirect topology, and maintains an open hierarchical community.

X.400 systems vary by implementation. GO-MHS (Global Open MHS) uses mostly static routing with published RELAY-MTAs and indirect topology. ADMD infrastructure (X.400 via carriers) uses static routing, indirect topology, and closed hierarchical communities with routing control. Long Bud (a pilot project using X.500 directories) moves toward dynamic routing with X.500-based rules. X42D (an experiment) uses DNS-based routing adapted for X.400.

Real-world email is a hybrid of approaches. Most organizations hide internal systems behind a firewall MTA, use default routes for outgoing mail, and run dynamic routing between major hubs. The choice of routing strategy depends on the organization's size, the email protocols in use, reliability requirements, and management preferences.
sections.eli5: Different email systems—Internet mail, UUCP, X.400—use different routing strategies. Some use static tables, others adapt dynamically. Some hide internal systems, others are wide open.
